item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: O Ministério das Relações Exteriores da Coreia do Norte afirmou, em comunicado publicado pela agência de notícias estatal KCNA, que a aprovação dos Estados Unidos para a construção do primeiro submarino nuclear da Coreia do Sul é “um desdobramento perigoso” que acrescentou nova instabilidade ao ambiente político e militar da região Ásia-Pacífico. A aprovação também é mais uma demonstração da proliferação nuclear dos EUA por meio do pacto Aukus, afirmou o ministério norte-coreano, traçando um histórico do que descreveu como o “acúmulo radical de armas nucleares” por parte de Washington, que resultou no “colapso da ordem nuclear internacional”. A Coreia do Sul pretende lançar seu primeiro submarino de propulsão nuclear em meados da década de 2030, no âmbito de um novo programa destinado a combater as ameaças nucleares e de mísseis lançados por submarinos da Coreia do Norte. O plano para o submarino nuclear de Seul foi acertado com Washington no âmbito de um acordo comercial firmado entre os dois aliados no ano passado.

item.title: Canada energy regulator approves Trans Mountain tolls settlement
item.description: The Canada Energy Regulator on Monday approved Trans Mountain's negotiated tolls settlement, finding the tolls just and reasonable and setting a new framework for tariffs and transportation services on the pipeline system.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: The Canada Energy Regulator on Monday approved Trans Mountain's negotiated tolls settlement, finding the tolls just and reasonable and setting a new framework for tariffs and transportation services on the pipeline system. The decision allows up to 90% of the pipeline's capacity to be contracted to shippers, up from 80%, the regulator said. The regulator said Trans Mountain can still ensure other shippers have meaningful access to available pipeline capacity. The settlement resolves an [USN:L6N439182 TEXT:"18-month dispute"] over tolls charged on the expanded pipeline, which began operations in 2024 after a C$34 billion ($23.98 billion) expansion. The expanded 890,000-barrels-per-day pipeline is Canada's only east-west oil pipeline and gives producers direct access to China and other Asian markets. No commercially interested parties opposed the negotiated settlement, the regulator said. Trans Mountain has proposed boosting capacity by up to 300,000 bpd through optimization projects by 2028 and earlier this year, launched a bidding process for roughly 90,000 bpd of new capacity. ($1 = 1.4176 Canadian dollars)

item.title: Anthropic's IPO prospectus shows sweeping AI vision, surging costs
item.description: Anthropic is making a massive bet that AI will transform the global economy more profoundly than industrialization, electricity and the internet, according to its IPO prospectus seen by Reuters. The public sale could value the startup at more than $2 trillion.
item.dc:creator: Echo Wang
item.content:encoded: Anthropic is making a massive bet that AI will transform the global economy more profoundly than industrialization, electricity and the internet, according to its IPO prospectus seen by Reuters. But the cost to get there will be staggering. Anthropic reported a net loss of $42 billion in 2025, and plans to spend $518 billion on cloud, computing and infrastructure obligations in coming years, according to the prospectus. Exclusive: Anthropic warns AI may pose 'existential risks to humanity' in IPO filing The prospectus details how the company has grown sharply in the last year — while also posting wider losses. Revenue grew 12-fold in 2025 to nearly $4.6 billion, even as the company lost more than $8 billion on an operating basis, excluding writedowns of various liabilities mostly tied to previous fundraising, according to the documents, reported here for the first time. The public sale, which could value it at more than $2 trillion, would capitalize on the rapid rise of the AI startup lab that only came into existence five years ago, and establish it as a benchmark for how Wall Street values AI's leading companies, including rival OpenAI. The plans come as Anthropic confronts evidence from its own research that increasingly autonomous AI models can behave in unexpected and potentially harmful ways, including sabotaging code, assisting fraud and manipulating information in controlled tests. Exclusive: Anthropic leaders to control AI lab via 'Founder LLC' to promote public good over market forces These reports have broken into the wider public sphere, igniting fears over how companies can keep the increasingly powerful systems under control as they race to deploy them commercially. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has called for the global AI community to slow the pace of releasing new capabilities to address those concerns. Still, Anthropic rolled out its new Opus 5.5 model last week to counter OpenAI’s momentum since its launch of GPT-6 Astra, ahead of its own expected IPO. The AI lab spent $7.33 billion on compute and infrastructure last year, a threefold surge from 2024, accounting for more than half of its $12.65 billion in total operating expenses. [USN:L6N45818P TEXT:"Anthropic's public market debut"] is likely to be pushed to after the November US midterm elections, Reuters previously reported, citing sources. The sale would bring public investors into an AI race that has been until now underwritten by venture capital firms, sovereign wealth funds and Big Tech companies. Anthropic declined to comment. A $2 TRILLION VALUATION EXPECTED Anthropic's expected valuation [USN:L6N4480X8 TEXT:"target"] is more than double its own estimated valuation of $965 billion in May. The near-$42 billion net loss included a roughly $34 billion accounting charge that reflected an increase in the estimated value of financing that could eventually turn into Anthropic shares, rather than money the company spent running its business. Anthropic said nearly a quarter of its revenue came from two customers last year, and as part of its risk factors, warned that many of its largest clients were not locked into long-term contracts and could cut or stop spending. Anthropic had cash, cash equivalents and short-term investments totaling $20.28 billion as of December 31, the prospectus shows. Anthropic's debut would follow SpaceX's (SPCX.O) [USN:L4N42G0A9 TEXT:"recent blockbuster"] IPO that valued Elon Musk's company at $1.77 trillion. That company's shares surged 19% in their June 12 debut to $160, but currently trade at around $147 -- above where the IPO sold at $135 apiece. That performance could give investors pause as they assess the still-lofty valuations for high-growth companies. AI and chip stocks have sold off recently, and Anthropic's sale will further test whether enthusiasm for the AI trade can withstand greater scrutiny, given its ambitious growth projections. Still, the listing stands to cap one of the strongest years for US IPOs since 2021, despite elevated interest rates, economic uncertainty and valuation concerns. THE TRILLION-DOLLAR AI RACE Anthropic's biggest challenger remains OpenAI, as the two firms fiercely compete for business customers, talent and influence in Washington. OpenAI [USN:L4N42A1M0 TEXT:"confidentially filed"] for an IPO in June. The ChatGPT maker is expected to list by early 2027, according to media reports. Anthropic was founded by researchers who left its rival after disagreements over governance and AI safety. It released its first large language model in [USN:L4N45K1CG TEXT:"March 2023"], competing directly with OpenAI. It also competes with SpaceX's xAI, Alphabet's (GOOGL.O) Google and Meta (META.O) to build out AI infrastructure. Analysts expect the first company to go public to establish valuation benchmarks for the AI industry and attract investors who have waited years for a pure-play way to bet on the technology. Amazon (AMZN.O) and Google were two of Anthropic's early key strategic partners. Both companies have invested billions of dollars into the startup while simultaneously supplying cloud infrastructure needed to train and deploy Claude models. Anthropic and CEO Amodei have clashed with the White House over the use of its tools, which led to [USN:L6N40C0YN TEXT:"the Pentagon temporarily blacklisting"] Anthropic, a move blocked by a US judge in August.

item.title: CONSOLIDA EUA e Irã conversam separadamente com mediadores na mais recente tentativa de pôr fim à guerra
item.description: Autoridades dos EUA e do Irã conversaram separadamente com mediadores nesta segunda-feira, como parte de um esforço renovado para pôr fim a sete meses de guerra, segundo autoridades de ambos os países.
item.dc:creator: Enas Alashray
item.content:encoded: Autoridades dos EUA e do Irã conversaram separadamente com mediadores nesta segunda-feira, como parte de um esforço renovado para pôr fim a sete meses de guerra, segundo autoridades de ambos os países. Espera-se que quaisquer novas negociações se concentrem em uma versão revisada da proposta de sete dias que o Irã apresentou na semana passada, à margem da Assembleia Geral das Nações Unidas, disse à Reuters uma autoridade a par das negociações. A guerra começou no final de fevereiro com ataques dos EUA e de Israel ao Irã, matando milhares de pessoas ao longo de sete meses e abalando os mercados globais, já que rotas marítimas vitais para o transporte de petróleo permaneceram bloqueadas. Os EUA e o Irã já haviam concordado duas vezes com cessar-fogos em negociações de paz mediadas, em abril e junho. Esses acordos se desintegraram rapidamente. O ministro das Relações Exteriores do Irã, Abbas Araqchi, que permaneceu em Nova York após participar da Assembleia Geral, disse que o Irã espera receber a resposta dos EUA às suas últimas propostas de cessar-fogo e às suas condições para restabelecer a passagem do tráfego marítimo no Estreito de Ormuz, segundo a agência de notícias estatal Irna. “Se os norte-americanos afirmam que estão buscando um acordo ou uma solução pacífica, nós apresentamos essa solução”, disse Araqchi. Autoridades norte-americanas conversaram separadamente com mediadores nesta segunda-feira, disse o presidente dos EUA, Donald Trump, a repórteres na Casa Branca, sem dar mais detalhes. TRUMP SINALIZOU NOVAS NEGOCIAÇÕES NESTA SEMANA O plano de sete dias do Irã prevê o fim de todas as hostilidades no Irã e no Líbano, o descongelamento de ativos iranianos no valor de bilhões de dólares, o fim das sanções ao petróleo iraniano e o levantamento do bloqueio dos EUA aos portos iranianos. O Irã permitiria então a reabertura do Estreito de Ormuz, uma rota vital para petroleiros, e os dois lados também retomariam as negociações sobre o programa nuclear iraniano e o desejo de Trump de apreender ou eliminar o urânio altamente enriquecido do país. Trump afirmou no sábado que havia rejeitado a proposta do Irã, alegando que o país buscava um acordo rápido devido à pressão econômica devastadora a que está sujeito. No entanto, ele também disse ao Axios no domingo que esperava que os negociadores dos EUA participassem de novas negociações nesta semana. Araqchi afirmou no domingo que os mediadores não haviam comunicado formalmente a rejeição dos EUA e que o Irã aguardava a posição definitiva de Washington antes de decidir seus próximos passos. “Nossas condições são claras, e qualquer medida para reabrir o Estreito de Ormuz depende do cumprimento dessas condições”, disse ele no domingo, acrescentando que somente uma solução negociada poderia resolver o impasse.

item.title: Meta taps Australia's Firmus for AI computing capacity in Southeast Asia
item.description: Australia's Firmus said on Tuesday it had signed AI infrastructure agreements with Facebook parent Meta Platforms for graphics processing unit compute capacity at its data centre facilities in Southeast Asia.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Australia's Firmus said on Tuesday it had signed AI infrastructure agreements with Facebook parent Meta Platforms (META.O) for graphics processing unit compute capacity at its data centre facilities in Southeast Asia. Here are some more details: Under the deal, Firmus will provide contracted capacity and expansion options built on Nvidia's full-stack DSX platform to support Meta's AI research, model development and training. Financial terms of the agreement were not disclosed. The deal builds on Meta's existing deployment of Nvidia GB300 NVL72 systems at Firmus' Melbourne data centre, the largest deployment of Blackwell Ultra systems in the Southern Hemisphere. Firmus designs, manufactures and operates AI factories to support large-scale workloads. The company is preparing for a [USN:L4N45F0GG TEXT:"$5 billion initial public offering"] to fund growth in AI projects, in what could be Australia's second-largest IPO.

item.title: At Warriors camp, Steph Curry raring to go, Kristaps Porzingis out again
item.description: Stephen Curry's contract is settled and his knee feels healthy as the Golden State Warriors prepare to decamp for Hawaii to kick off training camp.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Stephen Curry's contract is settled and his knee feels healthy as the Golden State Warriors prepare to decamp for Hawaii to kick off training camp. Curry signed a two-year contract extension on Friday worth $116 million, including a player option for the 2028-29 campaign. The four-time NBA champion has spent his entire career with the Warriors. "This is home," Curry said Monday at the team's preseason media day. "This is what we've built. This is a community that I've played in front of my entire career. Being able to finish the story the right way is a big part of what I can control." The Warriors' front office presented Curry with multiple options, including the maximum contract he was eligible for: a $136.7 million extension over two years. Curry left roughly $20.7 million on the table over the two-year extension. "Without knowing the answers to the test, it was my best way to study for it, if that makes sense," Curry said. "It's about for us to have a chance this season ... We're all smart people in this room. So you can kind of read the tea leaves on why it's designed the way that it is." Curry added that he isn't interested in "fast-forwarding" to the trade deadline or next offseason, instead focusing on preparing for his 18th NBA campaign. "If it's the alternative (and we aren't competitive), then you make decisions based off of that, too," Curry said. "I think for me (the contract decision) is how I've approached every opportunity in my career. You can't fast-forward your mind, or else you're not going to be to do your job as a player to try to win." The 12-time All-Star and 11-time All-NBA selection was limited to 43 games last season, including a 27-game absence because of a right knee injury that he insisted is no longer a concern. "Knee is feeling great, ready to go," Curry said. "No issues at all. There is a management element of it for sure where you just have to be mindful of everything that you're doing in practice, games, preparation. We haven't talked about the game schedule yet or anything like that where I'm kind of getting too far ahead of myself. But for training camp and the preseason schedule and getting myself into shape and ready to go, there's no limitations at all." It wasn't all rosy news for the Warriors, as general manager Mike Dunleavy announced that Kristaps Porzingis will be out "indefinitely" due to an unspecified health issue, which he was informed about only on Sunday. "So he'll miss the start of camp here. Don't have a timeline for him or anything further than that. So we're a little banged up to start, but we've got plenty of depth. We'll get through it." Dunleavy added that it was too soon to tell whether Porzingis would miss any game action. "He's just not available this week," the GM said. Golden State acquired Porzingis from the Atlanta Hawks at the 2026 trade deadline and signed him to a two-year, $40 million extension over the summer. But the one-time All-Star's weakness has been his availability; he's played more than 57 games just once in the past nine seasons, and he was limited to 32 games in 2025-26. Porzingis has battled a nervous system condition called POTS (postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome) for multiple years, but Dunleavy did not disclose whether that is what is currently sidelining him. "This came as a surprise," coach Steve Kerr said. "But we'll deal with it and move forward." --Field Level Media

item.title: UK shop price inflation slows despite costs pressures, BRC says
item.description: British shop price inflation slowed slightly in September despite rising costs pressures on retailers caused by the Iran war, according to a survey on Tuesday from the British Retail Consortium which urged the government to do more to help.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: British shop price inflation slowed slightly in September despite rising costs pressures on retailers caused by the Iran war, according to a survey on Tuesday from the British Retail Consortium which urged the government to do more to help. "Retailers have absorbed wave after wave of extra costs, but there is a limit to what businesses can shoulder," BRC Chief Executive Helen Dickinson said. "With higher business rates set to hit in April, alongside rising employment costs, energy bills and packaging taxes, the budget is a fork in the road." Finance minister John Healey could help to keep prices down in his October 28 tax and spending plan by helping retailers with their business rates bills, she said. The BRC survey showed: Annual shop price inflation fell to 1.4% in September from 1.5% in August but was slightly above the three-month average of 1.3% Food price inflation slowed to 2.5% from 2.8% as promotions helped bring down meat and dairy prices although poor harvests in Europe pushed up fruit prices and high commodity prices kept chocolate and confectionary prices elevated Non-food inflation slowed to 0.8% from 0.9% as strong discounting reduced the cost of back-to-school essentials The BRC survey was based on prices collected between September 1 and September 7 Britain's broader official consumer price inflation index [USN:L8N45806W TEXT:"rose to 3.1% in August"] and is [USN:L8N4590W3 TEXT:"expected to surpass"] 4% in early 2027 due to the energy price shock caused by the Iran war.

item.title: Ukraine's Zelenskiy says North Korea prepares to deploy another 10,000 troops to Russia
item.description: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said on Monday there are more than 8,000 North Korean troops on Russian territory and preparations are underway to deploy another 10,000 troops.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said on Monday there are more than 8,000 North Korean troops on Russian territory and preparations are underway to deploy another 10,000 troops. Citing "new data" on the deployment of North Korean troops to Russia, Zelenskiy said in a post on X they were "being selected for training and subsequent deployment to Russia." The Ukrainian president [USN:L6N44602S TEXT:"said"] in August that up to 50,000 North Korean soldiers could be sent to fight for Russia, and called on South Korea to provide support for Ukraine's air defence. South Korea [USN:P8N41X04T TEXT:"announced"] in July a $100 million aid package for Ukraine, although it excluded lethal weapons. Zelenskiy's comments on Monday came after Seoul and Kyiv were at odds over his [USN:L1N45G00G TEXT:"announcement"] last week that Ukraine had transferred two captured North Korean soldiers to South Korea. Seoul expressed regret over his announcement, citing an agreement to keep the transfer confidential. South Korea also [USN:L1N45K0AD TEXT:"protested"] against what it called a false statement from the Ukrainian presidential office denying that such a confidentiality agreement existed. North Korea has sent an estimated 14,000 to 15,000 troops to support Russia's war in Ukraine since 2024, according to Ukrainian and South Korean estimates, with most deployed in the Kursk region to help repel a Ukrainian incursion. Pyongyang has also supplied Russia with millions of artillery and mortar rounds, as well as ballistic missiles, long-range artillery systems and multiple-launch rocket systems, according to Ukrainian and independent assessments.

item.title: Waldron long seen as next Goldman CEO. The question is when
item.description: John Waldron has long been seen as successor to Goldman Sachs CEO David Solomon. The question was when the transition would happen.
item.dc:creator: Saeed Azhar
item.content:encoded: John Waldron has long been seen as successor to Goldman Sachs (GS.N) CEO David Solomon. The question was when the transition would happen. The Wall Street Journal reported on Monday that the investment bank had discussed a plan for Solomon to step down as CEO and be replaced with Chief Operating Officer Waldron as soon as next year, citing people familiar with the matter. "Of course the board regularly discusses succession, as we disclose in our filings, but there is no definitive timeline for succession at Goldman Sachs. Any assertions about timing are just speculation," Tony Fratto, Goldman's global head of communications, said in a statement. Solomon, 64, had been expected by senior staff to do 10 years in the CEO role, meaning he would likely stay in the position until 2028, a source familiar with the matter told Reuters on Monday. He was named CEO in October 2018. CEO succession has become a key focus for investors across Wall Street. At JPMorgan Chase (JPM.N) , attention has centered on when Jamie Dimon may step aside, while investors have also monitored leadership planning at Bank of America (BAC.N) under Brian Moynihan, one of the longest-serving chiefs among major US banks. Waldron, 57, has been expected to take over the reins from Solomon, sources familiar with the matter have said previously. His standing was further reinforced last year when he was [USN:L3N3PH1X8 TEXT:"appointed to the board"] and awarded a retention bonus. Wells Fargo analyst Mike Mayo said Goldman Sachs' succession has been 'unusually telegraphed' and Waldron's ascension has been expected since last year, when he was awarded the retention bonus. It is unlikely that Waldron changes the bank's strategy devised by Solomon. "They have been driving Goldman's priorities together," Mayo said. OVERSEEING LEADERS OF BANK'S MAIN DIVISIONS The Wall Street bank, which has been the top-ranked mergers and acquisitions adviser for two decades, has focused on growing its global banking and markets division, and wealth and asset management. Goldman Sachs [USN:L4N43G16H TEXT:"exceeded"] second-quarter profit expectations as dealmaking picked up and market volatility amid the US-Iran war boosted equities revenue to a record. Solomon significantly scaled back the firm's consumer banking by shedding assets after its foray into retail banking flopped. Waldron, who has been president and chief operating officer since October 2018, oversees the leaders of the bank's main divisions. He previously served as co-head of investment banking, a role he assumed in 2014 after joining Goldman in 2000. Goldman shares were little changed in after-hours trading. According to the WSJ report, discussions have involved Waldron taking over around the end of 2027 or in 2028. Under the plan, Solomon would remain executive chairman for one to two years after stepping down from the CEO role, the report said. The proposal would require approval from the bank's board, and its timing could change, it said. The report added that approval could happen in the coming months.

item.title: Trump government ads draw scrutiny weeks before midterm elections
item.description: Taxpayer-funded television ads featuring President Donald Trump, including spots celebrating a "golden age of America" and one accompanied by a chorus singing "love me" on repeat, are drawing bipartisan criticism and legal questions five weeks before midterm elections.
item.dc:creator: Helen Coster, Dawn Kopecki, Bo Erickson
item.content:encoded: Taxpayer-funded television ads featuring President Donald Trump, including spots celebrating a "golden age of America" and one accompanied by a chorus singing "love me" on repeat, are drawing bipartisan criticism and legal questions five weeks before midterm elections. The three nationally broadcast ads, ending with the disclaimer "Paid for by the US Government," have prompted ethics experts and lawmakers from Trump's fellow Republicans and rival Democrats alike to question whether public funds are being used to promote the president politically. Critics say the campaign may violate longstanding restrictions on government propaganda and political activity, while the White House has defended the spots as "public service announcements" intended to promote patriotism rather than campaign ads. Running ahead of midterm elections on November 3 that could reshape the balance of power in Washington, the ads tout American exceptionalism. One includes the president saying “America will never be a communist country” as a chorus sings “love me” in the background. A second combines images of Mount Rushmore with shots of Trump on stage as he praises “the golden age of America.” A third describes “the final battle,” with Trump pledging to demolish the deep state “with you by my side.” The "final battle" ad is nearly identical to one of Trump's campaign spots from 2024, with the exception of the disclaimer at the end. The ads have appeared during both “Saturday Night Live” and NFL football games on Sunday. They are the latest example of Trump flouting longstanding rules meant to prevent presidents from using the office for political gain, said Richard Painter, who served as the chief White House ethics lawyer under former President George W. Bush. "It's not the kind of thing the United States government lawfully can pay for under federal statutes,” he said. Criticism has also come from prominent members of Trump's own party. “I like the message," Senate Majority Leader John Thune told reporters on Monday, "but it shouldn't be paid for with taxpayer dollars.” The White House did not respond to Reuters questions about which government agency is paying for the ads, their cost and the critique that they are an improper use of public money. On its website last week, where the White House described them as “public service announcements,” it called them "a reminder for Americans to love their country and know why it’s worth defending." 'PROPAGANDA' Washington first banned domestic propaganda in response to the rise of communism in Europe in the 1940s "to make sure the United States doesn't start doing what authoritarian regimes do," said Painter, now a law professor at the University of Minnesota. "Glorification of the president himself, that's one telltale sign of propaganda," according to Painter, who said he also looks for attacks on political enemies and the absence of a clear policy issue. "Put all that together," he said, and the ads are "clearly propaganda." The ad campaign likely violates the 1939 Hatch Act, which prohibits government employees from engaging in campaign activities at work, according to Painter and other legal experts. Critics say previous Hatch Act allegations involving Trump's administration resulted in watchdog findings but little accountability, reflecting the challenges of imposing penalties on an uncooperative White House. "It seems to be a fairly clear-cut violation of legal prohibitions against public money being used for campaign purposes," said David Hopkins, an associate professor of political science at Boston College. It was unclear why the administration would use public funds for the campaign in an election cycle where Republicans have a clear fundraising advantage. Republican-aligned groups have reserved at least $888 million in advertising over the coming weeks, compared to at least $666 million for Democrats, according to AdImpact, which tracks political advertising. “You can’t spend public money to promote yourself,” Republican Senator John Kennedy from Louisiana said on "CBS Sunday." “Never take another Republican seriously when they pretend they care about 'waste, fraud and abuse,'" Democratic Senator Chris Murphy wrote on X. Charlie Black, a Republican political strategist who has worked on multiple presidential campaigns, said Trump's insistence on putting himself front and center could backfire on his party. History shows "if a president is unpopular, the more visible they are, the worse the party does," Black said. "He might beat the odds, and defy history, but I doubt it."

item.title: OpenAI shelves new AI model release over safety concerns
item.description: OpenAI has scrapped the release of GPT-6.1 Astra, a next-generation AI model planned for an October debut, after internal testing found the system did not meet the company's safety and alignment standards, the ChatGPT maker confirmed on Monday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: OpenAI has scrapped the release of GPT-6.1 Astra, a next-generation AI model planned for an October debut, after internal testing found the system did not meet the company's safety and alignment standards, the ChatGPT maker confirmed on Monday. OpenAI Chief Executive Sam Altman and rival Anthropic's CEO Dario Amodei earlier this month joined [USN:L4N456128 TEXT:"industry leaders"] in calling for a slower pace of AI development and stronger safety measures. OpenAI has warned that Astra, its flagship GPT-6 model, can at times evade human oversight, while the company and rivals such as [USN:L6N45L00B TEXT:"Anthropic"] have faced scrutiny over experimental AI systems that breached safeguards, including an OpenAI model that accessed Australia's health system database. The Wall Street Journal reported earlier in the day that OpenAI had abandoned plans to launch the model, which was expected to be integrated into ChatGPT and Codex and was designed to handle more complex tasks without human assistance. The Journal reported that GPT-6.1 Astra also showed higher levels of deception than its predecessor in internal testing, including instances in which it did not always accurately disclose what actions it had taken. "While (GPT-6.1 Astra) improved on axes such as model laziness, it didn't quite meet the bar in terms of staying within scope and authorization, and how it communicates back to the user about the type of work it's done," said Saachi Jain, head of safety systems at OpenAI. "Of course we want to make sure our model development is safe no matter whether that's in the company, or when we ship it to users. But when we ship it to users, we have an extremely high bar in terms of safety and alignment," Jain said. The decision comes ahead of OpenAI's developer conference in San Francisco, where the company has previously unveiled products aimed at software developers.

item.title: Retooled Celtics forge into unknown after Jaylen Brown trade
item.description: A week after their president of basketball operations said that breaking up their longtime star duo was "inevitable," the Boston Celtics faced life after Jaylen Brown as they kicked off the preseason at their media day Monday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: A week after their president of basketball operations said that breaking up their longtime star duo was "inevitable," the Boston Celtics faced life after Jaylen Brown as they kicked off the preseason at their media day Monday. Celtics coach Joe Mazzulla began the day by remarking on "an eventful offseason" and thanking Brown, who was traded to the Philadelphia 76ers for Paul George and a collection of draft picks. "I want to pay my respects to Jaylen and everything he represented for this organization and the community over the last 10 years," Mazzulla said. "Obviously, what he's been able to accomplish has been great, and it's not a one-time thing to where you let go of that. There's obviously a short-term perspective and then a long-term perspective about what he did over the course of his time here, both on and off the court, and that should not be forgotten. "At the same time, today is the first day of our 2026-27 season, and shifting our focus towards the players and that team and the season that we have." Brown and Jayson Tatum had been teammates since the Celtics drafted Tatum third overall in 2017. Their nine-year partnership produced one championship (2023-24), another NBA Finals trip (lost to the Warriors in 2022), and an extended run as the cream of the crop in the East. But after Brown led the Celtics for most of last season while Tatum recovered from Achilles surgery, their tenure together fizzled out in the form of a first-round playoff dismissal at the hands of the 76ers. Brad Stevens, the head of Boston's front office, said in a SiriusXM interview last week that trying to play through both ball-dominant players wasn't a sustainable long-term path. "At the end of the day, the biggest thing is that when evaluating how the team played in the past couple of playoffs, we have to build the depth to stay competitive as we can to build for a long, sustainable run; it was inevitable," Stevens said. "For us, it was a really hard decision. There were a lot of things that went into it. You have two max players, two max usage; those are the things you have to make a decision on. ... Jaylen's a great player, but I like the team we have." For his part, Tatum spoke highly of Brown in his press availability Monday. "It's tough, obviously," Tatum said. "I always say, the business of the NBA always comes in and plays a part, always, and I've seen it throughout my 10 years of being in this league. For me, I'm just grateful for what we accomplished and what he meant to this city and this organization. Just the ups and downs in our career that we were able to grow and learn from and that made us the players we are today." In an Eastern Conference that features the defending champion New York Knicks, the Miami Heat with Giannis Antetokounmpo and the Philadelphia 76ers with Brown and LeBron James joining Joel Embiid and company, the Celtics also move forward as a retooled unit. Tatum, Derrick White and Payton Pritchard will get to work with George, new center Mitchell Robinson and veteran Mike Conley Jr. "The thing I'm most excited about is the unknown," said Mazzulla, who made clear this summer that he had no input on the decision to trade Brown. "I always get excited about that because there's risk to the unknown and there's also opportunity to the unknown -- what we can become, what we have to go through to get to where we want to get to. I'm inspired and motivated by the unknown more than anything else because I don't know what we can be." Mazzulla also joked that the Celtics won't be able to foul Robinson anymore, a reference to Boston's strategy of constantly sending Robinson to the line when he played for New York. In fact, Robinson told reporters that he demanded an apology when Mazzulla visited him in Nashville this summer. "At first, we had a little issue," Robinson said. "I'm like, ‘You've got to say sorry for fouling me.' If he didn't want to do that, then we would have had some issues. But, he apologized and we're on the same team now, so it's going to be great. Just continuing to build and get to know him as the year goes on." --Field Level Media

item.title: AstraZeneca to invest $2 billion in Summit Therapeutics for cancer drug tie-up
item.description: Summit Therapeutics said on Monday that British drugmaker AstraZeneca would invest $2 billion in the company and collaborate on a series of studies testing their cancer treatments together.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Summit Therapeutics (SMMT.O) said on Monday that British drugmaker AstraZeneca (AZN.L) would invest $2 billion in the company and collaborate on a series of studies testing their cancer treatments together. Summit's shares rose over 15% in extended trading following the announcement. Here are some details: AstraZeneca will buy preferred shares in Summit at an equivalent price of $18.36 per common share, representing an 18.6% premium to Summit's Monday closing price of $15.48. The investment marks a major vote of confidence in ivonescimab, a next-generation cancer treatment [USN:L4N32W2GR TEXT:"licensed"] by Summit from China's Akeso (9926.HK) . Ivonescimab works by simultaneously blocking PD-1, which helps cancer evade the immune system, and VEGF, which tumors use to grow blood vessels, helping the immune system better find and attack cancer cells. As part of the partnership, the two companies will also launch clinical trials combining ivonescimab with AstraZeneca's cancer treatments. They have also signed a preliminary agreement to explore testing ivonescimab with several other AstraZeneca medicines, including its antibody-drug conjugates, a class of treatments that deliver cancer-killing drugs directly to tumor cells. The transaction is expected to close by the end of the week.

item.title: Juiz impede Trump de vincular verbas para combate ao terrorismo a mudanças eleitorais
item.description: Um juiz federal bloqueou, nesta segunda-feira, o governo Trump de condicionar a liberação de verbas para o combate ao terrorismo destinadas a governos estaduais e municipais à implementação de mudanças na administração eleitoral.
item.dc:creator: Luc Cohen
item.content:encoded: Um juiz federal bloqueou, nesta segunda-feira, o governo Trump de condicionar a liberação de verbas para o combate ao terrorismo destinadas a governos estaduais e municipais à implementação de mudanças na administração eleitoral. A decisão do juiz federal Amir Ali, de Washington, marca a mais recente derrota do presidente Donald Trump em sua tentativa de aumentar a autoridade do governo federal sobre as eleições antes das eleições de meio de mandato de 3 de novembro, quando o Partido Republicano luta para manter a maioria nas duas Casas do Congresso. No início deste ano, o Departamento de Segurança Interna (DHS) anunciou que reteria 20% dos recursos destinados a programas de subsídios relacionados à preparação para ataques terroristas e outras ameaças até que os governos estaduais ou locais adotassem medidas de administração eleitoral defendidas pelo governo. Em sua decisão nesta segunda-feira, Ali deu razão aos condados e cidades do Texas, Ohio e Tennessee, que entraram com uma ação para bloquear as mudanças, alegando que a imposição de condições para a liberação desses recursos excedia a autoridade da Agência Federal de Gestão de Emergências (Fema). Uma coalizão de Estados governados em sua maioria por democratas entrou com uma ação judicial separada contra a diretriz, que ainda está pendente. Os programas de subsídios, que totalizam cerca de US$1,1 bilhão, já existem há anos. Nenhum deles foi concebido especificamente com a segurança eleitoral em mente. “O Congresso não autorizou que o programa de subsídios fosse usado para o tipo de reformas na administração eleitoral que a Fema exige neste caso — mudanças que, sejam elas válidas ou não do ponto de vista político, não são propostas para preparar ou responder a ‘atos de terrorismo’”, escreveu Ali, nomeado pelo presidente democrata Joe Biden. Nem o DHS nem o Departamento de Justiça (DOJ), que representa o governo federal na Justiça, responderam imediatamente aos pedidos de comentário. Ao anunciar o plano para condicionar os recursos, o secretário do DHS, Markwayne Mullin, afirmou que os novos requisitos protegeriam os sistemas eleitorais contra interferências estrangeiras e ataques cibernéticos. O plano exigiria que os beneficiários das verbas utilizassem equipamentos que aceitassem cédulas de papel preenchidas à mão, em vez de sistemas de votação eletrônica, auditassem manualmente pelo menos 5% das cédulas depositadas e comparassem suas listas eleitorais com um banco de dados do DHS para garantir que nenhum não-cidadão estivesse registrado para votar. Trump há muito tempo faz alegações falsas sobre fraude eleitoral generalizada nas eleições dos EUA, incluindo a eleição presidencial de 2020, na qual foi derrotado. Estudos e auditorias independentes constataram que a fraude eleitoral é rara.

item.title: China risks swinging the tax pendulum too far
item.description: For decades, entrepreneurs quietly parked assets offshore in Hong Kong and beyond. Beijing’s fresh scrutiny of this hoard will raise revenue for the government and reshape stock markets. It also risks crushing animal spirits in a fragile economy.
item.dc:creator: Ka Sing Chan
item.content:encoded: Traditional Chinese wisdom warns against showing off wealth. For decades, the country’s entrepreneurs followed that advice by quietly parking assets offshore in Hong Kong and beyond. Now Beijing looks determined to bring those riches into the tax net to shore up government revenue. But the crackdown also risks crushing animal spirits in a fragile economy. Although Beijing says its recent actions merely bring existing tax laws into effect and address ambiguities, in practical terms they mark a significant shift in the treatment of overseas assets. The timing is hardly accidental. Since the property market bubble burst in 2021, local governments have lost roughly 4.5 trillion yuan ($630 billion) of annual land-sale revenue. At the same time, ever larger sums of Chinese wealth have accumulated offshore, creating an obvious potential tax base. Since May, authorities have fined offshore brokers including Futu (6FHAy.F) , and ordered a wind-down of their mainland clients' accounts, tightened disclosure requirements for overseas banking arrangements, and sharpened oversight of outbound investments. Beijing has also clarified that China’s 20% individual income tax applies to offshore trusts, and tax authorities have begun levying taxes on insurance policy income earned offshore. Taken together, what unnerves China’s wealthy is not any single measure but the pace of change and the fear it can upend an implicit bargain under which business owners could make money at home and protect it overseas and a potential blurring of the line between tax collection and capital controls. The campaign comes just as offshore Chinese wealth has reached unprecedented levels. Hong Kong has overtaken Switzerland as the world's largest cross-border wealth hub, with $2.9 trillion under management, about 60% tied to mainland money, according to a Boston Consulting Group report published in April. Mainland Chinese and Hong Kong investors' holdings of US equities have roughly doubled in five years. HSBC Life, Hong Kong's largest life insurer, collected HK$24 billion from just 1,516 single-premium policies in the first half of this year. The average ticket size of over $2 million reflects strong demand from affluent clients for products often used for succession planning and investment diversification. Meanwhile, China's capital and financial-account deficit, a broad measure of capital outflow, exceeded $800 billion in 2025, reflecting that a growing share of wealth is being stored abroad. The bigger problem is uncertainty. Wealthy families are scrambling to assess the impact of the new trust rules, including how far Beijing will look back and how assets in them will be valued. A broader question looms if this marks the start of a new tax era under President Xi Jinping’s ‘Common Prosperity’ drive. Several advisers, including former central-bank chief Guo Shuqing, have recently advocated for the introduction of an inheritance tax , for example. Markets are offering a preview of the impact. Besides a [USN:L4N443043 TEXT:"slump"] in shares of insurers including AIA (1299.HK) and Prudential (PRU.L) , this month hotpot chain Haidilao International's (6862.HK) shares fell after co-founder Shu Ping sold about HK$2.75 billion, roughly $350 million, of stock through a family trust vehicle. The company said the disposal reflected personal financial needs. As well as stock sales, Chinese entrepreneurs are also looking to borrow against their shares to fund tax bills, bankers have told Breakingviews. Advances in data sharing, reporting requirements and artificial-intelligence tools have made offshore assets far easier to identify and trace. Still, Beijing’s crackdown may raise large sums of money without yielding all the benefits policymakers hope for. Assets held under trusts in Hong Kong reached HK$6.2 trillion in 2025, according to Hong Kong’s Securities and Futures Commission. If these are taxed at 20%, authorities will pocket $159 billion. That’s impressive but only a fraction of the lost annual land sales revenue. And if authorities also hope to convince people to invest their money onshore, they may be disappointed too: China's stock market remains one of the world's chronic underperformers. The biggest danger is that an abrupt shift in taxing wealth could reduce the incentive to create it in the first place. Beijing has long tolerated legal grey zones when they served broader economic goals. For example, offshore listings of China’s internet tech champions Tencent (0700.HK) and Alibaba (9988.HK) relied on variable-interest-entity structures that allowed foreign investors to gain economic exposure to a Chinese company without owning the Chinese operating business. It gave founders access to foreign capital and hard currency, though it sat awkwardly alongside foreign ownership restrictions. But that bargain, and the exit door it offered, appears to be narrowing. Beijing told the co-founders of Manus not to leave China this year before forcing the AI startup to unwind its agreed $2 billion sale to Meta Platforms (META.O) . As well as tightening oversight of outbound investment, authorities have tightened rules on cross-border movement by individuals deemed to threaten national security or violate technology-export controls. One number to watch will be the exodus of wealthy individuals attempting to move beyond China's tax net. Investment-migration consultancy Henley & Partners estimates that China saw a net outflow of 7,800 millionaires carrying roughly $55.9 billion of investable wealth last year, even as the United States attracted a net inflow of 7,500. Ultimately Beijing may be less concerned about where money goes than ensuring it does not disappear from view. Officials have reiterated Hong Kong's role as an international financial centre and continue to call for further opening of China's financial system. That would imply capital can continue to move, provided officials can see where it goes and claim a share. Most entrepreneurs can live with a 20% tax, but the sudden increased scrutiny of the well-heeled and uncertainty over where Beijing will draw the final lines on issues from offshore wealth to mobility will keep many on their guard. Chinese residents will have to pay a 20% income tax on income derived from transferring assets into offshore trusts, as well as income generated during the lifetime of such trusts, the Ministry of Finance and the State Taxation Administration jointly announced on July 24.
